stem: A unit test YAML definition for `dim_customers` has both a `given:` block and an `expect:` block. A developer needs to know exactly which of the two actually supplies the mock input rows for the test's referenced models, versus which one states what the model should produce. What does `given` specify?

option_texts.A: The mock input rows for each `ref()` or `source()` listed under it, which the model's logic then transforms
option_texts.B: The expected output rows that the model should produce after transformation
option_texts.C: A list of column names the test should ignore when comparing actual and expected output
option_texts.D: The warehouse connection details the unit test should use instead of the project's default target

drill_answer_short: given supplies the mock input data; expect supplies the expected output
decision_hinge: given: # the mock data for your inputs - input: ref('stg_customers'). expect: # the expected output given the inputs above.

plausible_options.B: versus which one states what the model should produce

eliminated_by.C: needs to know exactly which of the two actually supplies the mock input rows for the test's referenced models
eliminated_by.D: needs to know exactly which of the two actually supplies the mock input rows for the test's referenced models

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — that is exactly what the expect block specifies, not given
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — unit tests have no documented column-ignore list under given
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — given supplies mock data rows, not connection configuration

stem: A team wants a genuine, documented advantage of unit tests over traditional data tests like `not_null` and `unique`, specifically around catching a logic bug before it ever reaches real data. What is that documented advantage?

option_texts.A: Unit tests validate modeling logic against a small set of static inputs before the full model is ever materialized in production
option_texts.B: Unit tests run faster before anything else, because they skip compiling any SQL at all
option_texts.C: Unit tests replace the need for data tests entirely, since they check the same things more efficiently
option_texts.D: Unit tests automatically test every model in the project without being explicitly defined anywhere

drill_answer_short: Unit tests validate logic against static inputs before the model is materialized, unlike data tests
decision_hinge: Unit tests allow you to validate your SQL modeling logic on a small set of static inputs before you materialize your full model in production. Historically, dbt's data tests could only be executed after building a model.

plausible_options.C: specifically around catching a logic bug before it ever reaches real data

eliminated_by.B: A team wants a genuine, documented advantage of unit tests over traditional data tests
eliminated_by.D: A team wants a genuine, documented advantage of unit tests over traditional data tests

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — unit tests still compile and run SQL against the static fixture rows
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — unit tests and data tests check different things at different times; neither makes the other redundant
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — unit tests must be explicitly defined in a YAML file under model-paths

stem: A project has `unique` and `not_null` declared under a column in `schema.yml`, and also has a `.sql` file in `tests/` with a single `select` statement. A developer needs to know the fundamental difference in how dbt treats these two kinds of definitions. What's the real difference?

option_texts.A: The `schema.yml` entries are generic tests built from a parameterized `test` block; the standalone file is a singular test, which is just the raw SQL that returns failing rows
option_texts.B: The `schema.yml` entries only run during `dbt build`, while standalone SQL files only run during `dbt test`
option_texts.C: The standalone SQL file must also declare `model` and `column_name` as arguments, just like a generic test
option_texts.D: Both are functionally identical; dbt simply stores one in YAML and one in SQL for organizational preference

drill_answer_short: schema.yml entries are generic tests from a test block; the standalone file is a singular test with no block
decision_hinge: A generic data test is defined in a test block, which contains a parameterized query and accepts arguments. A singular data test is the exact SQL that will return failing records, defined in a .sql file, typically in your tests directory.

plausible_options.D: the fundamental difference in how dbt treats these two kinds of definitions

eliminated_by.B: has `unique` and `not_null` declared under a column in `schema.yml`, and also has a `.sql` file in `tests/`

C.signal: has `unique` and `not_null` declared under a column in `schema.yml`, and also has a `.sql` file in `tests/`
C.requires_fact: A singular data test is the exact SQL that will return failing records; only a generic test's test block accepts model and column_name as arguments.

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — both generic and singular tests run under either dbt test or dbt build, the command does not depend on which kind it is
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated fact — a singular test needs no test block and no declared arguments at all
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — the two formats have genuinely different mechanics, not just a different file location

stem: A column is tested with `accepted_values: values: ['t', 'f']`, written at the top level without an `arguments:` key. A reviewer needs to evaluate two claims about this configuration against current dbt documentation. Which TWO statements are correct?

option_texts.A: This top-level form still works as a supported alias, though nesting `values` under `arguments:` is the currently recommended form
option_texts.B: `accepted_values` only validates non-null values in the column; null values are not checked against the list
option_texts.C: `accepted_values` also requires every value listed in the arguments against the column to appear at least once
option_texts.D: Writing `values` outside an `arguments:` block like this causes an immediate parse error on all current dbt versions

drill_answer_short: Top-level values still works (older form); accepted_values only checks non-null values
decision_hinge: accepted_values: arguments: values is available in v1.10.5 and higher; older versions can set the argument name as the top-level property. This data test validates that all of the non-null values present in a column are present in a supplied list.

plausible_options.C: written at the top level without an `arguments:` key

eliminated_by.D: written at the top level without an `arguments:` key

distractor_traps.C: T8: scope error — the test checks that present values are allowed, not that every allowed value must appear
distractor_traps.D: T6: stale behaviour — the top-level form is older but still supported as an alias, not rejected outright

stem: A model-level test compares row counts between two models, using a generic test macro that is not one of dbt's four built-in tests, and that the team never wrote themselves. The team needs to know the documented, current source of additional generic tests like this one. Where do they come from?

option_texts.A: Additional generic tests have been open-sourced in packages, such as the `dbt-utils` package, which you make available in your project through package management
option_texts.B: dbt automatically ships every possible additional generic test out of the box, so none of them ever come from a package
option_texts.C: Such a test can only exist if the team wrote it themselves as a custom generic test in `macros/`
option_texts.D: dbt Cloud exclusively provides these additional tests, and they are unavailable in dbt Core projects

drill_answer_short: Additional generic tests are open-sourced in packages like dbt-utils, installed via packages.yml
decision_hinge: Out of the box, dbt ships with unique, not_null, accepted_values, and relationships. Some additional generic tests have been open-sourced in the dbt-utils package. Check out the docs on packages to learn how to make these tests available in your project.

plausible_options.C: that the team never wrote themselves

eliminated_by.B: that is not one of dbt's four built-in tests, and that the team never wrote themselves
eliminated_by.D: that is not one of dbt's four built-in tests, and that the team never wrote themselves

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says this test is not one of the four dbt ships out of the box
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — a team can write its own custom generic test, but packages are the other documented source, and the stem rules out self-authorship
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — package-sourced generic tests are available in dbt Core, not exclusive to dbt Cloud

stem: A `unique` test on `order_id` needs to run only against rows where `order_id > 21`, ignoring older rows entirely, while still keeping its default `severity`. The team needs the correct config key for this narrowing, not a property that happens to sound similar. Which config achieves it?

option_texts.A: `where`, a framework option nested under `config` that adds a filter clause limiting which rows the test considers
option_texts.B: `filter`, a property available on every generic test for limiting which rows it scans
option_texts.C: `limit`, which caps the number of failing rows returned without changing which rows are scanned
option_texts.D: `severity`, since adjusting this config also narrows which rows a test evaluates

drill_answer_short: where is the documented config for narrowing which rows a data test considers
decision_hinge: You can add a config block for options like severity or where. unique: config: where: "order_id > 21". The config and where clause are optional.

plausible_options.B: needs to run only against rows where `order_id > 21`, ignoring older rows entirely

eliminated_by.C: needs the correct config key for this narrowing, not a property that happens to sound similar

D.requires_fact: You can add a config block for options like severity or where; where is the documented key for limiting which rows a test considers, separate from severity.

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — dbt's documented row-filtering config for generic tests is named where, not filter
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — a row-count limit on failures is a different concern from which rows feed into the test query
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — severity decides pass/warn/error, it does not change which rows a test scans

stem: A team sets both `store_failures: true` and `store_failures_as: "view"` on the same test. They need to know which of the two configs actually wins, and what it controls that the other one doesn't. What's the real relationship between them?

option_texts.A: `store_failures_as` takes precedence and controls the storage format (ephemeral, table, or view); `store_failures` only controls whether failures are stored at all
option_texts.B: `store_failures` takes precedence and controls over `store_failures_as` whenever both are set on the same test
option_texts.C: The two configs are redundant aliases that each control the same setting, so setting both has no additional effect
option_texts.D: `store_failures_as` only applies to singular tests, while `store_failures` only applies to generic tests

drill_answer_short: store_failures_as takes precedence and sets the storage format; store_failures only toggles storing at all
decision_hinge: store_failures_as is an optional config that specifies how test failures should be stored. If store_failures is also configured, store_failures_as takes precedence. The three supported values are ephemeral, table, and view.

plausible_options.C: They need to know which of the two configs actually wins, and what it controls that the other one doesn't

eliminated_by.B: A team sets both `store_failures: true` and `store_failures_as: "view"` on the same test

D.signal: A team sets both `store_failures: true` and `store_failures_as: "view"` on the same test
D.requires_fact: You can configure store_failures_as in all the same places as store_failures, including singular tests and generic tests, so neither is restricted to only one test kind.

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — store_failures_as is documented as taking precedence, not store_failures
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — the two configs are related but control different things: whether to store, and in what format
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — both configs are available in all the same places, not split by test kind

stem: A team wants to unit test an incremental model's logic for handling late-arriving data, and needs this to work for both a from-scratch build and an already-incremental run, without hand-rolling two separate test files. What testing approach does dbt actually document for this?

option_texts.A: Override the output of macros, vars, or environment variables in the unit test config to exercise the model in both full-refresh and incremental modes
option_texts.B: Unit tests cannot be applied to incremental models at all; only data tests can validate them
option_texts.C: Write two separate unit test files, one hardcoded for full-refresh and one hardcoded for incremental mode, since dbt cannot parameterize this
option_texts.D: Unit test only the final materialized table's shape, since unit tests cannot evaluate incremental logic before a build

drill_answer_short: Unit tests can override macros, vars, or env vars to exercise both full-refresh and incremental modes
decision_hinge: When configuring your unit test, you can override the output of macros, vars, or environment variables. This enables you to unit test your incremental models in full refresh and incremental modes.

plausible_options.D: needs this to work for both a from-scratch build and an already-incremental run

eliminated_by.B: wants to unit test an incremental model's logic for handling late-arriving data
eliminated_by.C: without hand-rolling two separate test files

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — dbt explicitly documents unit testing incremental models
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated requirement — the stem rules out hand-rolling two separate test files
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — unit tests validate modeling logic on static inputs before a build, which is exactly what enables testing incremental behavior pre-materialization

stem: A `room_type` column is tested with `accepted_values: arguments: values: ['Entire home/apt', 'Private room', 'Shared room', 'Hotel room']`. A new row arrives with `room_type = 'Boat'`, a value not in that list. The team needs to know exactly what the next `dbt test` run reports for this column.

option_texts.A: The test fails, returning the `Boat` row as a failing record, since its value is not in the supplied list
option_texts.B: The test automatically adds `Boat` to the accepted list going forward, so the next run passes
option_texts.C: The test passes, since `accepted_values` only checks the first value it finds in the column
option_texts.D: The test silently skips any row whose value was not already present when the test was first defined

drill_answer_short: A value outside the supplied list is returned as a failing row by accepted_values
decision_hinge: accepted_values validates that all of the non-null values present in a column are present in a supplied list of values. Data tests return a set of failing records; if a value disproves the assertion, that row is a failure.

plausible_options.D: A new row arrives with `room_type = 'Boat'`, a value not in that list

eliminated_by.B: The team needs to know exactly what the next `dbt test` run reports for this column
eliminated_by.C: The team needs to know exactly what the next `dbt test` run reports for this column

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — accepted_values never mutates its own configured list based on incoming data
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — accepted_values checks every non-null value in the column, not just the first one found
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — the test re-evaluates the full column on every run, it does not grandfather in pre-existing values
